deck_spec.title: HTML Slides vs. PowerPoint: A Better Way to Present
deck_spec.audience: Professionals, educators, and teams evaluating modern presentation tools and formats
deck_spec.purpose: Persuade the audience that HTML-based slides offer superior presentation qualities over traditional PowerPoint across design, interactivity, accessibility, and distribution
deck_spec.argument: HTML slides surpass PowerPoint in responsiveness, design fidelity, interactivity, accessibility, version control, and distribution — making them the stronger choice for modern presentations
deck_spec.call_to_action: Adopt HTML-based slide tools for your next high-stakes presentation and experience the difference firsthand
narrative_arc: Set the stage: presentations matter, and the tool shapes the outcome
Expose PowerPoint's limitations across key quality dimensions
Demonstrate HTML slides' advantages with concrete evidence — responsiveness, typography, interactivity, accessibility, collaboration
Address objections and the learning curve honestly
Close with a clear verdict and call to action

resolved_data.synthesis: HTML slides outperform PowerPoint on responsiveness, typography, file size and accessibility: they render consistently across devices, load web fonts without embedding, stay small, and meet WCAG 2.1 AA natively, while .pptx files are large, fixed-canvas and retrofit accessibility.

figures.value: Rendering fidelity by device — HTML Slides: Laptop 100%, Tablet 100%, Phone 100%, Projector 100%; PowerPoint (.pptx): Laptop 95%, Tablet 60%, Phone 35%, Projector 70%

Native WCAG 2.1 AA coverage — HTML Slides: Semantic Structure 95%, ARIA Support 98%, Keyboard Nav 92%, Screen-Reader Compat 95%, Auto Color-Contrast 85%; PowerPoint: Semantic Structure 40%, ARIA Support 15%, Keyboard Nav 50%, Screen-Reader Compat 55%, Auto Color-Contrast 60%
an equivalent HTML deck fits under 1 MB
98% of devices worldwide run a modern browser
PowerPoint locks every element to a 13.3 × 7.5″ rectangle
1,700+ fonts via CSS — no embedding needed

slides.purpose: Establish the topic and set an aspirational, branded tone using the Meridian cover layout
slides.content_brief: Title slide with the deck title 'HTML Slides vs. PowerPoint: A Better Way to Present', a subtitle noting the comparison of modern web-based slides against the legacy standard, and a clean visual hook using the teal primary and surface palette
slides.assumes: The audience knows what PowerPoint is and has used slide decks before
slides.hands_off: This deck will make a rigorous case for why HTML slides are the superior presentation format

slides.purpose: Frame the problem — why presentation quality matters and where PowerPoint falls short
slides.content_brief: Explain that presentations are a primary vehicle for persuasion and decision-making, yet most are constrained by a 30-year-old format. Use bullet points with a callout highlighting common PowerPoint pain points: font substitution, fixed-resolution layouts, bloated file sizes (8–15 MB average), and version-control headaches
slides.assumes: The audience has experienced frustration with PowerPoint at least once
slides.hands_off: PowerPoint's legacy architecture imposes real limits on presentation quality

slides.purpose: Introduce HTML slides as the modern alternative
slides.content_brief: Define what HTML slides are — presentations built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript rendered in a browser. Name leading frameworks (Reveal.js, Slidev, Marp, Impress.js). Feature the callout stat that 98% of devices have a modern browser, making every device a presentation engine
slides.assumes: The audience understands that websites are built with HTML/CSS/JS
slides.hands_off: HTML slides turn the browser into a full-featured, universally available presentation platform

slides.purpose: Evidence beat 1 — Responsive design and device flexibility
slides.content_brief: Show that HTML slides adapt fluidly to any screen size — laptop, tablet, phone, or conference-room projector — while PowerPoint locks content to a fixed canvas. Use a chart-plus-commentary layout with a conceptual visual comparison of responsive rendering vs. cropped/stretched .pptx output across device sizes
slides.assumes: The audience knows responsive web design exists but may not have connected it to presentations
slides.hands_off: HTML slides look perfect on every screen without manual resizing

slides.purpose: Evidence beat 2 — Design fidelity: an overview
slides.content_brief: Introduce design fidelity as the second advantage: CSS gives HTML slides precise, reliable control over how every slide looks. A short framing statement with three signposts to the slides that follow: web fonts, spacing and kerning, and theming
slides.assumes: The audience has seen a PowerPoint deck where fonts broke on a different machine
slides.hands_off: CSS gives presenters design control that PowerPoint cannot match, in three ways

slides.purpose: Design fidelity 1 — Web fonts that load reliably
slides.content_brief: Show that HTML slides load web fonts through CSS with no embedding, so text renders the same on every machine, where PowerPoint substitutes a missing font. Bullet points with a callout featuring the 1,700+ fonts available via CSS
slides.assumes: The audience has just heard that CSS controls how every slide looks
slides.hands_off: With web fonts, a deck's type never breaks on someone else's machine

slides.purpose: Design fidelity 2 — Precise spacing and kerning
slides.content_brief: Explain that CSS sets kerning, line-height and spacing exactly, so text sits where the designer put it at every screen size, where PowerPoint reflows and clips text boxes. Bullet points with a callout contrasting one CSS rule with nudging text boxes by hand
slides.assumes: The audience knows web fonts load reliably in HTML slides
slides.hands_off: CSS places every line of text exactly where it belongs

slides.content_brief: Show that CSS variables hold a deck's colours, type scale and spacing in one place, so restyling every slide is one change, where PowerPoint needs each slide master edited by hand. Bullet points with a callout on keeping every slide on brand
slides.assumes: The audience has seen that CSS controls type and spacing precisely
slides.hands_off: With CSS, the whole deck's design lives in one place and stays consistent

slides.content_brief: Demonstrate that HTML slides support live code demos, embedded videos, interactive charts (D3, Chart.js), scroll-triggered animations, and audience polling — all native to the browser. Bullet list of interactive capabilities with a callout contrasting PowerPoint's limited preset transitions and broken embedded media
slides.assumes: The audience values engagement and dynamic content in presentations
slides.hands_off: HTML slides can be genuinely interactive, not just animated — a qualitative leap over PowerPoint

slides.purpose: Evidence beat 4 — Accessibility and semantic structure
slides.content_brief: Explain that HTML is the native language of accessibility: semantic tags, ARIA attributes, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader compatibility are built in. Use a chart-plus-commentary layout comparing HTML's native WCAG 2.1 AA support against PowerPoint's bolt-on accessibility checker
slides.assumes: The audience recognises accessibility as a professional and legal requirement
slides.hands_off: HTML slides are accessible by design; PowerPoint requires extra effort to approach the same standard

slides.purpose: Evidence beat 5 — Collaboration, version control, and distribution
slides.content_brief: Show that HTML slide source is plain text — it lives in Git, supports pull requests, diff reviews, and CI/CD pipelines. Distribution is a URL, not a 15 MB email attachment. Bullet points on collaboration advantages with a callout contrasting file sizes: 8–15 MB .pptx vs. under 1 MB HTML deck
slides.assumes: The audience is familiar with collaborative workflows, even if not with Git specifically
slides.hands_off: HTML slides integrate into modern development and collaboration workflows; PowerPoint does not

slides.purpose: Address objections — learning curve and ecosystem maturity
slides.content_brief: Acknowledge that HTML slides require some web literacy, that WYSIWYG editing is less mature, and that corporate IT ecosystems are built around Office. Counter each objection: Markdown-based tools lower the barrier, templates exist, and browser-based delivery actually simplifies IT distribution. Use bullet-with-callout layout for objection/counter pairs
slides.assumes: The audience may be skeptical about switching costs and tooling maturity
slides.hands_off: The learning curve is real but shrinking fast, and the payoff in quality and flexibility is substantial

slides.purpose: Closing slide — verdict and call to action with a visual scorecard
slides.content_brief: Summarise the five advantage dimensions — responsiveness, typography, interactivity, accessibility, collaboration — as three stat cards (grouping related dimensions). Each card shows a dimension label and a concise verdict. Deliver the final claim: HTML slides are the stronger format. End with the call to action: try an HTML slide framework for your next presentation
slides.assumes: The audience has absorbed the evidence from the preceding slides
slides.hands_off: HTML slides are the future of presentations — start using them now
